figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Comparison of geometric update mechanisms. Conventional GFMs [88, 51, 95] use successive layer-specific transformations, tying their intermediate representations to layer depth. Recurrent-memory models [90, 21] process incoming frames while updating a persistent scene memory across observations. Although DéjàView [12] shares transformer weights, its updates remain conditioned on the refinement step. Solv3R applies the same stationary update operator regardless of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated.
figures.headline: Solv3R applies one stationary update at every iteration, whereas conventional models tie their intermediate states to layer depth.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Continuing geometric solving with new observations. When new views are introduced, Solv3R continues solving from its existing state, jointly refining both previously reconstructed and newly added views. DéjàView struggles to maintain consistent reconstruction. Numbers indicate camera rotation errors in degrees.
figures.headline: When new views join, Solv3R refines old and new views together, whereas DéjàView struggles to stay consistent.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Overview. Left: A stationary transformer block repeatedly updates the multi-view state through frame-wise and global attention, initial-state injection, and state normalization. Right: The same operator continues refining the reconstruction across solver calls, allowing new views to be introduced at any stage and jointly updated with existing views. Camera poses, depth maps, and ray maps can be decoded from the current state after any solver call.
figures.headline: A stationary transformer block updates the multi-view state across solver calls, and poses, depths and ray maps are decoded after any call.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Stable and corrective solver dynamics. Left: pose accuracy and relative state update norm over solver calls. DéjàView is trained with up to 16 steps (shaded). Middle: camera rotation error and relative state update aligned to the solver call at which each window meets the stopping criterion of 5, showing median and interquartile range. Right: rotation error at call 16 after perturbations at call 8 using relative (rel.) or fixed-scale (fixed) Gaussian noise, or state resets (reset).
figures.headline: Solv3R keeps camera error low as state updates shrink and recovers from noise or resets, whereas DéjàView does not.

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Warm-start convergence. Left: depth AbsRel along a KITTI [33] sequence, warm-starting each new frame from the previous solution with four solver calls. Right: percentage of new frames with rotation error below $2^{\circ}$ versus solver calls in a 24-view window, comparing warm-starting with restarting from scratch. Solv3R remains stable under continued warm-starting and achieves accurate camera estimates with fewer calls, whereas DéjàView diverges.
figures.headline: Solv3R stays stable under continued warm starts and needs fewer calls for accurate cameras, while DéjàView diverges.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Mixed-progress solving. Left: pose accuracy when each view is initialized from a randomly sampled reconstruction stage. Right: rotation error as each view progresses through a pipelined reconstruction window, where views enter and leave after each solver call. Solv3R maintains accurate reconstruction across views with varying reconstruction stages, whereas DéjàView is sensitive to their computational progress.
figures.headline: Solv3R stays accurate when views in a pipelined window are at varying reconstruction stages, whereas DéjàView is sensitive to progress.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Revising an existing reconstruction with new views. (a) Four views are solved for eight calls before twelve new views are introduced; camera colors indicate rotation error. (b,c) Median rotation error of the original and new views during continued refinement over 96 windows. Dashed curves in (b) indicate the no-join controls, where the original four views continue refinement for the same number of solver calls without introducing new views. Solv3R incorporates new views while improving existing camera estimates, whereas DéjàView fails to maintain a consistent reconstruction.
figures.headline: When new views join an existing reconstruction, Solv3R improves original camera estimates, while DéjàView fails to stay consistent.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Revisability and reuse. (a) Original-view rotation error when new views join at different refinement stages, compared with the no-join control; percentages indicate the fraction of improved windows. (b) Final pose accuracy versus total reconstruction time as the view set expands from 8 to 64. Solv3R improves existing estimates across different join times and achieves comparable accuracy to re-solving with less computation.
figures.headline: Adding views at different refinement stages improves original-view accuracy in most windows, at comparable accuracy to re-solving with less computation.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Relocalization against a frozen map. Green dots are query estimates within 5 cm and 5∘ of the ground truth (gray rings), and red crosses are the others, linked to their ground truth. Above each panel are the cache size per map view and the fraction of queries within 5 cm and 5∘. With the smallest cache, Solv3R localizes as many queries as the most accurate baseline.
figures.headline: Solv3R localizes as many frozen-map queries as the most accurate baseline while using the smallest cache.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 shows the queries of one scene, where DéjàView with a single cache scatters them while Solv3R places them where they belong.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Streaming reconstruction. Qualitative comparison with window-based reconstruction [26], recurrent-state methods [90, 21], and geometric-context approaches [18] on long sequences, with camera trajectories colored by position error.
figures.headline: Solv3R's streaming camera trajectories on long sequences are accurate compared with window-based and recurrent-state methods.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Streaming accuracy vs. efficiency. Comparison of online reconstruction methods in terms of geometric-mean pose ATE and per-frame runtime; bubble size indicates peak GPU memory. For Solv3R, S/L denotes small/large memory configurations, and numbers indicate solver calls per frame (L8 is the default).
figures.headline: Solv3R's online accuracy and per-frame runtime trade off across solver-call settings and memory configurations.
citing_sentences: As shown in , Solv3R achieves strong results across camera pose, video depth, and 3D reconstruction, with competitive runtime and low memory consumption. further illustrates accurate camera trajectories over long sequences, while Figure 12 shows the accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Stopping calls. Left: number of windows per stopping call, for the 144 of the 148 windows of the stability analysis that reach $\gamma=0.02$, stacked by dataset. Right: rotation error of each window at its stopping call.
figures.headline: Stopping calls for 144 windows fall between 13 and 32, and 143 of them have rotation error below 5 degrees.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Initialization of new views. Median rotation error of a newly arrived frame over solver calls, for 656 frames per dataset, 41 from each of 16 sequences. The new frame starts from its initial state $\mathbf{z}^{0}$, from $\mathbf{z}^{0}$ plus the solved offset of the previous frame (Offset), or from the solved state of the previous frame (Previous state). The frames that remain in the window keep their solved states. “From scratch” solves the whole window from the initial states.
figures.headline: Initializing a new frame from its previous solved state is compared with two other starts over solver calls.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Initialization in streaming. ATE of on-arrival predictions with the L8 window for different numbers of calls per frame. Each new frame starts from its initial state $\mathbf{z}^{0}$ (cold start) or from $\mathbf{z}^{0}$ plus the solved offset of the previous frame (warm start).
figures.headline: Warm-starting each streamed frame is compared with cold-starting it across different solver-call counts per frame.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Memory on a long sequence. GPU memory over the 2000 frames of the long office sequence of TUM RGB-D, on a logarithmic axis. All methods are evaluated on a single H100 GPU. Crosses mark where a method runs out of the 80 GB of GPU memory (gray dotted line).
figures.headline: Solv3R's memory levels off over 2000 frames, while two baselines run out of 80 GB at 320 and 365 frames.

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Attention across solver calls. We show the three global-attention heads, out of 12, that best find ground-truth correspondences at call 16. These are the same heads in Solv3R (left) and DéjàView (right). Top: fraction of query patches whose strongest attention in an adjacent view falls within one patch of the ground-truth correspondence. Bottom: similarity to the call-16 attention map, measured as the share of the call-16 attention mass on the 64 most attended keys of each call and normalized to 1 at call 16. The shaded range is the 16-step schedule of DéjàView. Averaged over 82 windows of ETH3D and ScanNet++.
figures.headline: Solv3R's best correspondence heads keep their attention near call 16, while DéjàView's correspondence accuracy falls below 3% by call 64.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Failure case. In this window, views 5–8 share little content with views 1–4. Solv3R places them at a wrong position and orientation within 16 calls and keeps them there up to call 64.
figures.headline: The failure case places views 5-8, which share little content with views 1-4, at a wrong pose that persists to call 64.
citing_sentences: The remaining window is shown in Fig. 18.

figures.label: Figure 19
figures.caption: Reconstructions that grow as views arrive. Each row shows one scene at three stages of one arrival pattern. Offline solves all views jointly, incremental adds the capture in thirds, streaming adds video frames one at a time, and arbitrary order adds random groups of views. Views that join continue the running solve, and the views already in it keep their states. Above each panel are the number of views in the solve and the number $K$ of solver calls run so far. Arrows give the views that joined, and orange marks their cameras.
figures.headline: The same solver reconstructs scenes whether views arrive offline, incrementally, as streamed frames, or in random groups.

figures.caption: One scene under the four arrival patterns. Shown as in Fig. 19. All four patterns end in nearly the same reconstruction, although the views arrive in different orders and receive different numbers of calls.
figures.headline: One scene under four arrival patterns ends in nearly the same reconstruction despite different view orders and call counts.

figures.caption: Offline reconstruction comparison. All methods see the same 100 images at once. VGGT, DA3-L, and VGGT-$\Omega$ misplace the second room, while Solv3R reconstructs both rooms in one piece.
figures.headline: Baselines misplace the second room of a 100-image scene, while Solv3R reconstructs both rooms in one piece.

Insets show the predicted cameras in color and the reference cameras in gray, seen from above. Solv3R places the cameras closest to the reference, while VGGT and VGGT-$\Omega$ fold the room.

abstract: Classical structure-from-motion reconstruction proceeds iteratively, refining camera poses and scene geometry from a current estimate. This allows maps to easily expand without recomputing already computed views, or geometry estimates to improve as more observations are provided. Most geometric foundation models, however, predict entire geometry in a single forward pass or update a recurrent state as frames arrive sequentially, making this expansion and refinement non-trivial. We introduce Solv3R, a looped transformer that learns to continue solving multi-view geometry from its current state. Importantly, its update operator is independent of the iteration count, allowing previously refined and newly introduced views to be jointly updated regardless of how “solved” they are. We train the operator to preserve accurate reconstructions under continued iteration and correct inaccurate states, enabling refinement of fixed image collections and integration of new observations. Representations of solved views can also be cached once and reused as geometric context across iterations, enabling compact and efficient key-value caching. We analyze the solver dynamics and compare it with the state-of-the-art, demonstrating that a single learned solver supports offline reconstruction, incremental reconstruction, relocalization, and streaming without task-specific training or modules. The code and models will be made publicly available at https://ubc-vision.github.io/solv3r/.

sections.body: The section motivates Solv3R. Feed-forward geometric foundation models predict geometry in one pass, so adding views typically means processing the combined image set again. Streaming models are limited to views that arrive sequentially. Classical structure-from-motion instead refines existing estimates as views arrive. The authors argue that a learned model should continue solving from its current state. They cite DéjàView as a looped model that shares weights but still conditions each block on the refinement step. Solv3R is proposed as a stationary learned update that supports offline reconstruction, added views and streaming in one architecture, with a key-value cache for solved views that is reused across solver calls.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Feed-forward geometric models struggle to refine or extend reconstructions, so the paper proposes Solv3R, a reusable learned solver.

sections.body: The related work covers geometric foundation models that predict poses and dense geometry from multiple views, and learned iterative refinement used in optical flow, stereo and visual SLAM. It also covers equilibrium and recurrent models, persistent scene memories, causal attention with caching, and window-based registration. The authors position Solv3R against DéjàView, which introduces shared recurrent computation for multi-view reconstruction, and say they extend it to continued solving across fixed and evolving view sets. Unlike separate streaming pipelines, Solv3R applies the same geometric solver to both offline and online reconstruction.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Related work spans feed-forward geometry, looped refinement and streaming reconstruction, which Solv3R applies as one solver.

sections.body: The method fine-tunes the shared transformer block of DéjàView so that its update does not depend on the iteration index. At every call the operator receives the current state and the encoded input images, and the updated state is rescaled to a fixed root-mean-square norm. Two changes remove the iteration dependence: learned constant gates replace step-conditioned gates, and a single scale factor normalizes the whole state. Training runs a random number of gradient-free solver calls, followed by differentiable calls, with Gaussian noise and view resets as perturbations. Supervision is applied at calls between the 24th and 48th, and predictions after 16 calls are distilled from DéjàView to preserve its priors.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A stationary learned update, trained for stability, correction and continuation, is shared across all solver calls.

sections.body: This section tests the solver properties against DéjàView. Refinement is measured by the relative state update $r^{k}$ between consecutive calls, and it stops when $r^{k}$ falls below 0.02. Of 148 windows, 144 meet this criterion within 64 calls, and 143 of these (99.3%) have camera rotation errors below 5°. When the state is perturbed at call 8 with Gaussian noise or view resets, Solv3R recovers accurate poses by call 16, whereas DéjàView does not. When each view starts from a random reconstruction stage, Solv3R's camera rotations differ by a mean of 0.08° across trials. Warm-start results show that Solv3R reaches accurate cameras in fewer calls than restarting from scratch.
sections.heading: Solver analysis
sections.headline: Solv3R's camera error stays low as updates shrink and recovers after perturbation, unlike DéjàView.

sections.body: Training fine-tunes the pretrained DéjàView block with AdamW at a learning rate of 2×10^-5 and an exponential moving average of the weights, for about one week on 8 H100 GPUs. Offline, Solv3R retains accuracy comparable to DéjàView at the same 16-call budget. Adaptive stopping with a threshold of 0.02 and at most 64 calls improves nearly all reconstruction metrics over fixed-budget inference, using only 3–4 additional calls on average. In incremental tests, twelve new views join four solved views, and original-view camera accuracy improves. For map-based relocalization on 7-Scenes, Solv3R reaches a recall of 72.8 at 5 cm and 5° with a cache of 2.86 MB per view. In streaming, Solv3R's TUM-dyn. ATE is .015 at 95 ms per frame, with 5.0 GB peak memory, and uses no streaming-specific training.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: Solv3R's accuracy at 16 calls is comparable to DéjàView, and it is competitive across offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion restates that Solv3R combines a stationary update operator with stable and corrective dynamics. The authors state that one learned solver covers offline and incremental reconstruction, map-based relocalization and streaming, without task-specific modules or a separate optimization backend. They frame the result as a path toward open-ended reconstruction in which estimates are continuously refined and revised as observations change. They suggest the perspective could extend to vision-language models, robotics and world modeling. This section reports no new experiments, so its claims rest on the earlier results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The conclusion argues that a single learned solver can unify offline, incremental, relocalization and streaming reconstruction.

sections.body: The architecture details cover learned constant gates, a shared block with the initial state injected at each call, RMS normalization, 117M parameters, and images whose longer side is 504 pixels. The appendix lists the training data mixture and a two-stage schedule, along with the streaming configuration L8, which uses anchors, memory frames and a check every four incoming frames. Evaluation protocols cover stability, warm-start, pipelined and random-history tests, plus offline, incremental and relocalization setups. Further analyses cover attention heads, insertion order and a failure case with two view groups that have little overlap. Aerial results report an AUC@3 of 48.9 for Solv3R on Rubble and 22.5 on Building.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists implementation details, evaluation protocols, extra analyses, a failure case and additional aerial and qualitative results.
